newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel defends policies in parliament, blames SPD.
newsitem.headline: Waigel defends policies in parliament, blames SPD.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel defended the government's policies at a special session of parliament on Friday and blamed the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) for blocking efforts to cut taxes and unemployment.

Waigel told the lower house of parliament tax revenues for 1997 would be 18 billion marks ($10.6 billion) less than expected because of low inflation, increased efforts by Germans to cut taxes and efforts by companies to shift a greater portion of their profits abroad.
"We not let anyone knock us off our concept for the urgently needed reforms," Waigel said. "We will stick with our policies to promote growth and overcome the current problems."
Waigel said the problems, in particular the high unemployment levels, could be best resolved if the SPD would cooperate with the government on a tax reform programme.
"The SPD has done nothing but torpedo our efforts to reform. You block everything we do," Waigel said.
He urged the SPD to return to the negotiating table with the government on working out a tax reform plan.
"You left because you were not ready for compromise," he said. "If you were interested in helping the unemployed, we could have an agreement within days."
Waigel also said that Germany would not exceed the deficit level laid down by the Maastricht Treaty for the single European currency.
"We will not go over three percent (ratio of deficit to gross domestic product)," Waigel said.
Waigel also said it was "right and proper" to use Bundesbank gold reserves to offset old debt.
"This is not a trick but normal practice," Waigel said.
He did not mention using gold reserves to reduce running deficit levels.
